TLDR (and TODO)

  • High-level goal: Our previous experiment gave us some decoding operators. We want to showcase its capabilities. For that purpose, we’ve picked the Moritz et al. paper.
  • How did Mortiz et al. perform analysis?
    • the lmer code is for calculating \(p\)-values for hypothesis testing.
    • the graphs are actually descriptive summary statistics in distributional form.
  • What is Mortiz’s plan of analysis here (as in, are they trying to model an average participant? Something else??)

Repeating Mortiz’s analysis

#point arc
exp2_dotArc <- read.csv(
  here("data", "moritz", "exp", "exp2-point-arc.csv"),
  ,
  check.names = FALSE
)
#point
exp2_dotX <- read.csv(
  here("data", "moritz", "exp", "exp2-point.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
exp2 <- rbind(exp2_dotArc, exp2_dotX) %>%
  as_tibble(.) %>%
  select(assignmentid, mark, flip, variability, normalized_error)

Perform the correction:

Code 
exp2 %>%
  group_by(assignmentid, mark) %>%
  mutate(subj_mean = mean(normalized_error)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(grand_mean = mean(normalized_error)) %>%
  mutate(corrected = normalized_error - subj_mean + grand_mean) %>%
  group_by(mark, variability) %>%
  summarise(
    mu = mean(normalized_error),
    se = sd(corrected) / sqrt(n()) * sqrt(2 / (2 - 1)), # k is 2
    .groups = "drop"
  )

Generate posterior predictions for an “average” participant

Here are the details of the original experiment:

  • Hypothesis: “the effect of variability will be smaller for graphs with points spaced along the x-axis than graphs with points spaced along the arc” (Moritz et al., 2023, p. 5) (pdf)
  • Experiment Design:
    • Within Subject:
      • 2 variability: 0 and 0.4
      • 2 flipped1: upper and lower
    • Between Subject:
      • 3 mark type: line, cartesian spaced points, arc spaced points
        • Note that we will only use cartesian spaced points and arc spaced points for replication.
    • 12 different seeds for randomization -> 2 * 2 * 12 = 48 trials per participant.

1 i.e., whether the plot was flipped or not, where flip == FALSE implies that upper-y region has more variability, and flip == TRUE implies that the lower-y region has more variability

Read in Stimuli Data

First, read in the stimuli data from Mortiz experiment 2:

Code 
exp_json_data <- jsonlite::fromJSON(here(
  "data",
  "moritz",
  "stimuli",
  "exp2-stimuli.json"
)) %>%
  as_tibble(.)

stimuli_df <- exp_json_data %>%
  select(index, seed, noise, flip, type, data) %>%
  mutate(noise = as.character(noise))

# get the mapping between og index and the index used in exp
stimuli_df %>%
  filter(type == "point") %>%
  mutate(expIndex = 1:nrow(.)) %>%
  select(index, type, expIndex) -> point_map
stimuli_df %>%
  filter(type == "point_arc") %>%
  mutate(expIndex = 1:nrow(.)) %>%
  select(index, type, expIndex) -> pointArc_map

# calculate the answer
stimuli_df <- stimuli_df %>%
  filter(type != "line") %>%
  unnest(data) %>%
  left_join(point_map, by = join_by(index, type)) %>%
  left_join(pointArc_map, by = join_by(index, type)) %>%
  mutate(expIndex = coalesce(expIndex.x, expIndex.y)) %>%
  select(index, expIndex, type, flip, noise, seed, x, y) %>%
  ungroup(.) %>%
  rename(ogIndex = index, num.x = x, num.y = y)
stimuli_df

Define helper functions:

Code 
get_og_stimuli <- function(i) {
  mean <- stimuli_df %>%
    filter(ogIndex == i) %>%
    pull(num.y) %>%
    mean(.)

  stimuli_df %>%
    filter(ogIndex == i) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = num.x, y = num.y)) +
    geom_point() +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = mean, color = "gray", linetype = "dashed") +
    annotate("text", x = 120, y = mean, label = mean) +
    labs(title = paste0("ogIndex", " ", i))
}

# return visual angle in degrees and not radian
vis_angle <- function(size, distance) {
  return(2 * atan(size / (2 * distance)) * 180 / pi)
}

# define function for turning vis angle to phy size
phys_size <- function(va, distance) {
  return(2 * distance * tan(va * pi / 360))
}

Let’s also read in the data collected from pilot:

NoteA note on translating between spaces

The goal is to translate from the pixel space to the physical space, and then to the visual angle space.

  1. Data to Pixel: This should be given by the custom VegaEmbed component we built (directly fetching)
  • In this case, data is from \(x \in [0, 120]\) and \(y \in [0, 1]\) with the x-axis mapping to 500 px and y-axis to 200 px.
  1. Pixel to Physical: need to know the pixel to MM ratio, which is different per Participant.
  2. Physical to Vis Angle: need to know the distance to screen, again, which is different per Participant.
Code 
raw_df <- read_csv(here("data", "part_2", "part2_pilot.csv")) %>% as_tibble(.)

pilot_df <- raw_df %>%
  select(
    participantId,
    trialId,
    trialOrder,
    responseId,
    answer,
    duration,
    parameters_taskid,
    parameters_params
  )

# visual angle related participant-level data
participant_df <- pilot_df %>%
  filter(!responseId %in% c("numericResponse", "pixelResponse")) %>%
  group_by(participantId) %>%
  filter(
    responseId %in%
      c(
        "prolificId",
        "pixelsPerMM",
        "dist-calibration-MM",
        "dist-calibration-CM",
        "ball-positions",
        "square-position"
      )
  ) %>%
  select(participantId, responseId, answer) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = responseId, values_from = answer) %>%
  # we will not use participants who have distance calibration < 250 mm
  mutate(`dist-calibration-MM` = as.numeric(`dist-calibration-MM`)) %>%
  filter(`dist-calibration-MM` >= 250) %>%
  select(1, 3, 4) %>%
  rename(distToScreen = `dist-calibration-MM`) %>%
  mutate(
    pixelsPerMM = as.numeric(pixelsPerMM),
    distToScreen = as.numeric(distToScreen)
  )

# only keep people whose ans are somewhat useful
keep_id <- participant_df %>% pull(participantId)

# responses
resp_df <- pilot_df %>%
  filter(responseId %in% c("numericResponse", "pixelResponse")) %>%
  select(participantId, trialId, responseId, answer) %>%
  separate_wider_delim(
    col = trialId,
    delim = "_",
    names = c("type", NA, "index")
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = "responseId", values_from = "answer") %>%
  mutate(
    numericResponse = as.numeric(numericResponse),
    pixelResponse = as.numeric(pixelResponse),
    index = as.integer(index)
  ) %>%
  rename(expIndex = index) %>%
  mutate(pixelResponse = 200 - pixelResponse + 5) %>%
  # only keep the ones that matter
  filter(participantId %in% keep_id) %>%
  left_join(participant_df) %>%
  rename(
    num.y = numericResponse,
    px.y = pixelResponse,
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    pixelsPerMM = as.numeric(pixelsPerMM),
    phy.y = px.y / pixelsPerMM,
    va.y = vis_angle(phy.y, distToScreen)
  )

participant_df <- resp_df %>%
  count(participantId, type) %>%
  select(-n) %>%
  left_join(participant_df) %>%
  mutate(type = ifelse(type == "point", type, "point_arc"))

And then we also calculate the answer dataframe ans_df. Note that we are using the same strategy that Mortiz et al. used to calculate error and normalized error2.

2 … which is, instead of calculating the actual mean across 60 points for each trial, for trials that share the same value for seed and flip, they share the same “default mean”, i.e., the mean of the point type, instead of its actual mean.

Code 
temp_df <- stimuli_df %>%
  filter(type == "point") %>%
  group_by(seed, flip) %>%
  summarise(num.ans.y = mean(num.y)) %>%
  ungroup(.)

ans_df <- stimuli_df %>%
  select(-num.x, -num.y) %>%
  group_by(ogIndex, expIndex, type, flip, noise, seed) %>%
  summarise(.) %>%
  ungroup(.) %>%
  left_join(temp_df)

ans_df

Read in fitted model for project_to_y_axis

Recall the we defined the following model for the “project from dot to axis” operator:

\[ \begin{align*} \texttt{error}_i &\sim \mathcal{N}(\beta_0 + u_{\text{PID[i]}}, \sigma_{i, \text{PID}[i]}) \\ \log(\sigma_{i, j}) &= \alpha_j + \log(\texttt{va.ans.x}_i) \\ \text{or:} \log(\sigma_{i, j}) &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_\alpha + \log(\texttt{va.ans.x}_i), \sigma_\alpha)\\ \alpha_j &\sim N(\mu_\alpha, \sigma_\alpha) \\ \mu_\alpha &\sim N(0, 1) \\ \sigma_\alpha &\sim \mathcal{N}^+(0, 1) \end{align*} \]

Here is the specification we used for fitting:

# Recall that we defined error = resp - ans
f <- bf(
  error_va ~ (1 | participantId),
  sigma ~ (1 | participantId) + offset(log(va.ans.x))
)

p <- c(
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = Intercept),
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = sd, group = participantId, lb = 0),
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = Intercept, dpar = "sigma"),
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = sd, group = participantId, dpar = sigma, lb = 0)
)

And here we load the actual fitted model:

model <- readRDS(here("analysis", "fitted_models", "task5.y.rds"))
model
 Family: gaussian 
  Links: mu = identity; sigma = log 
Formula: error_va ~ 1 + (1 | participantId) 
         sigma ~ (1 | participantId) + offset(log(va.ans.x))
   Data: . (Number of observations: 160) 
  Draws: 4 chains, each with iter = 6000; warmup = 3000; thin = 1;
         total post-warmup draws = 12000

Multilevel Hyperparameters:
~participantId (Number of levels: 16) 
                    Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
sd(Intercept)           0.04      0.01     0.03     0.06 1.00     3545     6339
sd(sigma_Intercept)     0.31      0.11     0.12     0.54 1.00     3036     2946

Regression Coefficients:
                Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
Intercept           0.00      0.01    -0.02     0.03 1.00     2888     4584
sigma_Intercept    -4.63      0.10    -4.83    -4.42 1.00     4859     5913

Draws were sampled using sample(hmc). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).
NoteHow do things map to each other? 
model %>% get_variables(.) %>% head(4)
[1] "b_Intercept"                       "b_sigma_Intercept"                
[3] "sd_participantId__Intercept"       "sd_participantId__sigma_Intercept"
  • b_Intercept corresponds to \(\beta_0\)
  • b_sigma_Intercept corresponds to \(\alpha_0\)
  • sd_participantId__Intercept and sd_participantId__sigma_Intercept corresponds to \(\tau_\mu\) and \(\tau_\alpha\)
  • r_participantId[<id>, Intercept], r_participantId__sigma[<id>, Intercept] correspond to \(u_j\) and \(v_j\) respectively.

… with specific fixed pixelToMM and distToScreen

We will make the predictions for an average participant, conditioning on specific values of pixelToMM and distToScreen.

Note here that we are also implicitly making the assumption that the same participant saw both the point type condition and the point_arc type condition, which is NOT the case for the actual study.

Strategy 1 — Project to vertical line x==0

For a baseline strategy, we assume that the participant projects from the dot to the y-axis, and then performs some mental averaging.

First, we calculate the visual angle values for all the stimuli. This is the route from num -> px -> MM -> VA. This will allow us to make predictions of error in the visual angle space.

# assume that the value of pixelToMM and distToScreen is fixed
# we get the new_data to be crossed with posterior draws

pixelToMM <- 5.12
distToScreen <- 473

# 5760 rows = 2 (plot type) * 2 (noise type) * 2 (flipped or not) *
#  12 repeated measures * 60 points per graph
new_data <- stimuli_df %>%
  # calculate pixel values from numerical values
  mutate(px.x = 500 / 120 * num.x, px.y = 200 * num.y) %>%
  # calcuate physical values (in MM) from pixel values
  mutate(phy.x = px.x / pixelToMM, phy.y = px.y / pixelToMM) %>%
  # calculate visual angle
  mutate(
    va.ans.x = vis_angle(phy.x, distToScreen),
    va.ans.y = vis_angle(phy.y, distToScreen)
  )

Get (thinned) posterior draws:

# 3000 iterations per chain * 4 chains = 12,000 rows
# if we thin by k, then we get 12,000 / k rows
draws <- model %>%
  spread_draws(b_Intercept, b_sigma_Intercept) %>%
  as_draws_df(.) %>%
  thin_draws(thin = 2) # if too much we can also do thinning

Then we go the prediction route: VA -> mm -> px -> num:

pred <- draws %>%
  # every draw * every dot;
  # will result in 5760 * 3000 (thinned version) row
  expand_grid(new_data) %>%
  mutate(
    # mu = b_Intercept,
    sigma = exp(b_sigma_Intercept + log(va.ans.x)),
    # va.pred.error = rnorm(n(), mean = mu, sd = sigma),
    va.pred.error = rnorm(n(), mean = b_Intercept, sd = sigma),
    va.pred.y = va.pred.error + va.ans.y
  ) %>%
  # turn vis angle back to numerical values
  mutate(
    phy.pred.y = phys_size(va.pred.y, distToScreen),
    px.pred.y = phy.pred.y * pixelToMM,
    num.pred.y = px.pred.y / 200
  )

Now we “average”3 across the 60 dots for each trial:

3 Averaging Strategy vs. Median Strategy: “Equal number of points or line below and above. A strategy we did not anticipate was ensuring an equal number of points or line lengths above and below the judgment indicator. To indicate their responses, participants drug a line on the graph. By allowing participants to place a line directly on the graphs, participants could then easily count the number of points above and below the line. One participant simply wrote, “I tried to have the number of points above and below the line be approximately equal.” Unsurprisingly, this strategy was most common for participants who viewed graphs with points equally spaced along the x-axis (24%).” (Moritz et al., 2023, p. 7) (pdf)

avg_pred <- pred %>%
  group_by(ogIndex, expIndex, type, flip, noise, .draw) %>%
  summarise(
    # suppose participants can calculate mean
    num.pred.avg.y = mean(num.pred.y),
    # suppor participants use the median instead
    num.pred.median.y = median(num.pred.y),
  )
NoteHow many rows?

To calculate how many rows that pred has we need to look at these two other dataframes:

  • The draws dataframe has 3000 iterations / chain \(\times\) 4 chains \(\div k = 2\) = 6000 rows
  • The new_data dataframe has 96 trials \(\times\) 60 dots per trial = 5760 rows
  • Therefore pred is going to be 6000 \(\times\) 5760 = 34560000 rows

If we don’t consider rejection sampling, and just calculate the average across all 60 dots for each trial, we will have 34560000/60 = 576000 rows for avg_pred.

And now we plot the results:

Code 
plot_df <- avg_pred %>%
  ungroup(.) %>%
  left_join(ans_df) %>%
  mutate(
    error.median = num.pred.median.y - num.ans.y,
    norm.error.median = ifelse(
      flip == FALSE,
      num.pred.median.y - num.ans.y,
      num.ans.y - num.pred.median.y
    ),
    error.avg = num.pred.avg.y - num.ans.y,
    norm.error.avg = ifelse(
      flip == FALSE,
      num.pred.avg.y - num.ans.y,
      num.ans.y - num.pred.avg.y
    )
  )

plot_df %>%
  group_by(type, noise, .draw) %>%
  summarise(error = mean(norm.error.avg)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = error, y = noise, fill = type)) +
  stat_halfeye(alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Posterior normalized error (mean strategy)"
  )
plot_df %>%
  group_by(type, noise, .draw) %>%
  summarise(error = mean(norm.error.median)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = error, y = noise, fill = type)) +
  stat_halfeye(alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Posterior normalized error (median strategy)"
  )

As one can see, the above posterior error has very small variance. Median has slightly larger variance, but the “normalized error” goes negative.

plot_df %>%
  group_by(type, noise, .draw) %>%
  summarise(error = mean(norm.error.median)) %>%
  median_qi()

Strategy 2 — Project to vertical line where xintercept == 60 and then xintercept == 0

Instead of trying to sum over the results projected to the y-axis, we could have a result projecting to the middle point, i.e., where everyone projects to \(x = 60\), and then use that as an input to then project to the y-axis in order to potentially introduce more variance into the results.

Again, assume that we have fixed values for pixelToMM and distToScreen:

pixelToMM <- 5.12
distToScreen <- 473

# physical distance between vertical line with xintercept == 60 and xintercept == 0
phy.x_ref <- (500 / 120 * 60) / pixelToMM

# 5760 rows = 2 (plot type) * 2 (noise type) * 2 (flipped or not) *
# 12 repeated measures * 60 points per graph
new_data <- stimuli_df %>%
  # calculate pixel values from numerical values
  mutate(px.x = 500 / 120 * abs(60 - num.x), px.y = 200 * num.y) %>% # <- OR NEW (?)
  # calcuate physical values (in MM) from pixel values
  mutate(phy.x = px.x / pixelToMM, phy.y = px.y / pixelToMM) %>%
  # calculate visual angle
  mutate(
    # va.ans.x = vis_angle(abs(phy.x - phy.x_ref), distToScreen), # <- NEW STUFF
    va.ans.x = vis_angle(phy.x, distToScreen),
    va.ans.y = vis_angle(phy.y, distToScreen)
  )

Create the posterior draws:

rm(draws)

draws <- model %>%
  spread_draws(b_Intercept, b_sigma_Intercept) %>%
  as_draws_df(.) %>%
  # thin parameter set to 4 instead of 2
  # for more aggressive thinning
  thin_draws(thin = 2)

Combine the posterior with new data:

rm(pred)

# project to the middle axis
pred <- draws %>%
  # every draw * every dot;
  # will result in 5760 * 3000 (thinned version) row
  expand_grid(new_data) %>%
  mutate(
    # mu = b_Intercept,
    sigma = exp(b_sigma_Intercept + log(va.ans.x)),
    # va.pred.error = rnorm(n(), mean = mu, sd = sigma),
    va.pred.error = rnorm(n(), mean = b_Intercept, sd = sigma),
    va.pred.y = va.pred.error + va.ans.y
  ) %>%
  group_by(ogIndex, expIndex, type, flip, noise, .draw) %>%
  summarise(
    # assume participants use the mean for second projection
    va.mid_pred.y.avg = mean(va.pred.y),
    # assume participants use the median for second projection
    va.mid_pred.y.median = median(va.pred.y),
    .groups = "drop_last"
  )

# project from middle to the left axis
pred2 <- pred %>%
  left_join(draws) %>%
  mutate(
    # distance to y-axis is vis angle distance from x == 60
    sigma = exp(b_sigma_Intercept + log(vis_angle(phy.x_ref, distToScreen))),
    va.pred.error = rnorm(n(), mean = b_Intercept, sd = sigma),
    va.pred.y.avg = va.pred.error + va.mid_pred.y.avg,
    va.pred.y.median = va.pred.error + va.mid_pred.y.median
  ) %>%
  # turn vis angle back to numerical values
  mutate(
    phy.pred.y.avg = phys_size(va.pred.y.avg, distToScreen),
    phy.pred.y.median = phys_size(va.pred.y.median, distToScreen),
    px.pred.y.avg = phy.pred.y.avg * pixelToMM,
    px.pred.y.median = phy.pred.y.median * pixelToMM,
    num.pred.y.avg = px.pred.y.avg / 200,
    num.pred.y.median = px.pred.y.median / 200
  )

Check to see the posterior prediction for one graph (ogIndex == 4):

Code 
pred2 %>%
  filter(ogIndex == 4) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = va.mid_pred.y.avg, y = "x == 60")) +
  stat_halfeye() +
  stat_halfeye(aes(x = va.pred.y.avg, y = "x == 0")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(2.2, 2.8)) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean strategy; project to x == 60, then to x == 0",
    x = "Visual Angle of Predicted Y value"
  )
pred2 %>%
  filter(ogIndex == 4) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = va.mid_pred.y.median, y = "x == 60")) +
  stat_halfeye() +
  stat_halfeye(aes(x = va.pred.y.median, y = "x == 0")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(2.2, 2.8)) +
  labs(
    title = "Median strategy; project to x == 60, then to x == 0",
    x = "Visual Angle of Predicted Y value"
  )

So we are indeed seeing more variations. The median at x == 60 is just a bit wider than the mean at x == 60 but when projected to x == 0 they result in a similarly shaped distribution.

What would this variation result in changes in the numerical space?

phys_size(0.25, distToScreen) * pixelToMM / 200
[1] 0.05283469

So 5% on the [0, 1] scale.

  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black")
plot_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = error.median, y = noise, fill = type)) +
  stat_halfeye(alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Strategy on twice projected value on y-axis",
    x = "Numerical Normalized Error on y-axis"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.03, 0.09)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black")

The results are very similiar, except that the median strategy reads like the mean strategy but shifted to the left of the x-axis for a bit …

Compared to strategy 1, I think the variance here is a bit bigger …

plot_df %>% median_qi()

Recall that all the above is for a single participant with a particular value for pixelToMM and distToScreen. We should also be able to calculate it for all participants in the pilot.

Generate posterior predictions and average across participants

Recall this is the list of participants we have from pilot:

participant_df

Let us first do more aggressive thinning:

Code 
draws <- model %>%
  spread_draws(b_Intercept, b_sigma_Intercept) %>%
  as_draws_df(.) %>%
  thin_draws(thin = 20)

# 6 participant * 48 trials per participant * 60 dots per trial
# 17280 rows 
new_data <- participant_df %>%
  left_join(stimuli_df, relationship = "many-to-many") %>% 
  # calculate pixel values from numerical values
  mutate(px.x = 500 / 120 * num.x, px.y = 200 * num.y) %>%
  # calcuate physical values (in MM) from pixel values
  mutate(phy.x = px.x / pixelsPerMM, phy.y = px.y / pixelsPerMM) %>%
  # calculate visual angle
  mutate(
    va.ans.x = vis_angle(phy.x, distToScreen),
    va.ans.y = vis_angle(phy.y, distToScreen)
  )

new_data

Strategy 1 – Project once to y-axis

Build the posterior prediction:

rm(pred)

# 17280 rows * 600 draws per row 
# 1036800 
pred <- new_data %>% 
  expand_grid(draws) %>%
  mutate(
    sigma = exp(b_sigma_Intercept + log(va.ans.x)),
    va.pred.error = rnorm(n(), mean = b_Intercept, sd = sigma),
    va.pred.y = va.pred.error + va.ans.y,
    # back-convert using this participant's pixelToMM
    phy.pred.y = phys_size(va.pred.y, distToScreen),
    px.pred.y = phy.pred.y * pixelToMM,
    num.pred.y = px.pred.y / 200
  )

Again, the above number of rows is obtained by participant (6) * trials/participant (48) * dots/trial (60) * draws/dot (600). First, we want to get a sense of average value per trial, that is, now the dataframe should have participant (6) * trials/participant (48) * draw/trial (600).

To then average across participants mean that we have distinct trials (48 * 2) * draw/trial (600):

avg_pred <- pred %>% group_by(participantId, expIndex, type, flip, noise, .draw) %>% 
  summarise(
    num.pred.avg.y = mean(num.pred.y),
    num.pred.median.y = median(num.pred.y)
  ) %>% 
  group_by(expIndex, type, flip, noise, .draw) %>% 
  summarise(
    num.pred.avg.y = mean(num.pred.avg.y), 
    num.pred.median.y = mean(num.pred.median.y)
  )

The next step then is to get the data that is used to plot error:

plot_df <- avg_pred %>%
  ungroup(.) %>%
  left_join(ans_df) %>%
  mutate(
    error.median = num.pred.median.y - num.ans.y,
    norm.error.median = ifelse(
      flip == FALSE,
      num.pred.median.y - num.ans.y,
      num.ans.y - num.pred.median.y
    ),
    error.avg = num.pred.avg.y - num.ans.y,
    norm.error.avg = ifelse(
      flip == FALSE,
      num.pred.avg.y - num.ans.y,
      num.ans.y - num.pred.avg.y
    )
  )

Finally let’s plot to see if we can get similar results:

Code 
plot_df %>% group_by(type, noise, .draw) %>% 
  summarise(error = mean(norm.error.median)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = error, y = noise, fill = type)) +
  stat_halfeye(alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Across participants (median)",
    x = "median(norm.error.median)"
  )
plot_df %>%
  group_by(type, noise, .draw) %>%
  summarise(error = mean(norm.error.avg)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = error, y = noise, fill = type)) +
  stat_halfeye(alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Across participants (mean)",
    x = "mean(norm.error.mean)"
  )

We are getting errors going negative for point in this case.

Strategy 2 – project twice

This time we will build the posterior prediction a bit differently:

# 6 participant * 48 trials per participant * 60 dots per trial
# 17280 rows 
new_data <- participant_df %>%
  left_join(stimuli_df, relationship = "many-to-many") %>% 
  # calculate pixel values from numerical values
  mutate(px.x = 500 / 120 * abs(num.x - 60), px.y = 200 * num.y) %>% # <- DIFF 
  # calcuate physical values (in MM) from pixel values
  mutate(phy.x = px.x / pixelsPerMM, phy.y = px.y / pixelsPerMM) %>%
  # calculate visual angle
  mutate(
    va.ans.x = vis_angle(phy.x, distToScreen),
    va.ans.y = vis_angle(phy.y, distToScreen)
  )

# 17280 rows * 600 draws per row 
# 1036800 
pred <- new_data %>% 
  expand_grid(draws) %>%
  mutate(
    sigma = exp(b_sigma_Intercept + log(va.ans.x)),
    va.pred.error = rnorm(n(), mean = b_Intercept, sd = sigma),
    # first projection to x == 60 
    va.pred.y = va.pred.error + va.ans.y,
  ) %>% 
  group_by(participantId, expIndex, type, flip, noise, .draw) %>% 
  summarise(
    va.pred.avg.y = mean(va.pred.y),
    va.pred.median.y = median(va.pred.y), 
    .groups = "drop_last"
  )

# project from middle to left axis 
pred2 <- pred %>%
  left_join(draws) %>%
  mutate(
    # distance to y-axis is vis angle distance from x == 60
    sigma = exp(b_sigma_Intercept + log(vis_angle(phy.x_ref, distToScreen))),
    va.pred.error = rnorm(n(), mean = b_Intercept, sd = sigma),
    va.pred.y.avg = va.pred.error + va.pred.avg.y,
    va.pred.y.median = va.pred.error + va.pred.median.y
  ) %>%
  # turn vis angle back to numerical values
  mutate(
    phy.pred.y.avg = phys_size(va.pred.y.avg, distToScreen),
    phy.pred.y.median = phys_size(va.pred.y.median, distToScreen),
    px.pred.y.avg = phy.pred.y.avg * pixelToMM,
    px.pred.y.median = phy.pred.y.median * pixelToMM,
    num.pred.y.avg = px.pred.y.avg / 200,
    num.pred.y.median = px.pred.y.median / 200
  )

Then we go through the same process:

avg_pred <- pred2 %>% 
  group_by(expIndex, type, flip, noise, .draw) %>% 
  summarise(
    num.pred.avg.y = mean(num.pred.y.avg), 
    num.pred.median.y = mean(num.pred.y.median)
  )

Then get dataframe used for plotting error:

plot_df <- avg_pred %>%
  ungroup(.) %>%
  left_join(ans_df) %>%
  mutate(
    error.median = num.pred.median.y - num.ans.y,
    norm.error.median = ifelse(
      flip == FALSE,
      num.pred.median.y - num.ans.y,
      num.ans.y - num.pred.median.y
    ),
    error.avg = num.pred.avg.y - num.ans.y,
    norm.error.avg = ifelse(
      flip == FALSE,
      num.pred.avg.y - num.ans.y,
      num.ans.y - num.pred.avg.y
    )
  )

Then plot:

Code 
plot_df %>% group_by(type, noise, .draw) %>% 
  summarise(error = mean(norm.error.median)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = error, y = noise, fill = type)) +
  stat_halfeye(alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Across participants (median)",
    x = "median(norm.error.median)"
  )
plot_df %>%
  group_by(type, noise, .draw) %>%
  summarise(error = mean(norm.error.avg)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = error, y = noise, fill = type)) +
  stat_halfeye(alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Across participants (mean)",
    x = "mean(norm.error.mean)"
  )

Alright, this one has slightly bigger variance (for all mean strategies), but still, we are seeing negative values for the point case … It’s like if we shift the whole distributions to the right by 0.02 or something then the results will look really quite similar …

I need to ask Matt to clarify exactly what he meant by making “comparisons” here …
